<rules>

<transformation>
The input is treated as a tile map. The output is NxM times larger than the input (where the input is N rows x M cols). Each input cell at (BR, BC) with a non-zero value causes a copy of the full input to be placed in the corresponding NxM block of the output (at rows BR*N .. BR*N+N-1, cols BC*M .. BC*M+M-1). Each input cell with value 0 produces an all-zero block at that position.
</transformation>

<asp>
% Count distinct row/col indices — equals grid dimensions for 0-indexed inputs
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{R : input(R, _, _)}.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{C : input(_, C, _)}.

% Output is NR*NR rows and NC*NC cols (input tiled by itself)
output_cell(R, C) :-
    input(BR, BC, _), input(DR, DC, _),
    n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
    R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC.

1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Non-zero block: the sub-cell must equal the input value at the relative position
:- input(BR, BC, V), V != 0,
   input(DR, DC, TileColor),
   n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
   R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC,
   output(R, C, ActualColor), ActualColor != TileColor.

% Zero block: every sub-cell must be 0
:- input(BR, BC, 0),
   input(DR, DC, _),
   n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
   R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC,
   output(R, C, ActualColor), ActualColor != 0.
</asp>
</example_1>

<transformation>
The output is the same size as the input. Color-3 cells are unchanged. Non-3 cells (value 0) that are enclosed by color-3 walls — i.e., cannot reach the grid boundary via 4-connected movement through non-3 cells — are filled with color 4. All other non-3 cells remain 0.

<asp>
% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- input(R, C, _).
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Grid boundary coordinates
min_row(R) :- R = #min{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
max_row(R) :- R = #max{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
min_col(C) :- C = #min{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.
max_col(C) :- C = #max{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.

% 4-connected adjacency offsets
delta(0,1). delta(0,-1). delta(1,0). delta(-1,0).

% Non-3 cells on the grid boundary are reachable from outside
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_row(Rmin), R = Rmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_row(Rmax), R = Rmax.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_col(Cmin), C = Cmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_col(Cmax), C = Cmax.

% Flood-fill outward through non-3 cells
outside(R2, C2) :-
    outside(R1, C1), delta(DR, DC),
    R2 = R1+DR, C2 = C1+DC,
    input(R2, C2, V), V != 3.

% Color-3 cells stay 3
:- input(R, C, 3), output(R, C, Color), Color != 3.

% Outside non-3 cells stay 0
:- outside(R, C), output(R, C, Color), Color != 0.

% Interior non-3 cells (enclosed by 3s, not reachable from boundary) become 4
:- input(R, C, 0), not outside(R, C), output(R, C, Color), Color != 4.
</asp>

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  ARC‑AGI transformation – tiling the whole input map into blocks.
%  The input grid has size (NR rows) × (NC cols).
%  Every input cell (BR,BC) creates an NR×NC block in the output:
%      – if the source cell value is 0 → the whole block is 0;
%      – otherwise the block is an exact copy of the whole input.
%  The output grid therefore has size (NR·NR) × (NC·NC).
% --------------------------------------------------------------

% 1.  Dimensions of the input (these are constants for a given instance)
nr(NR) :- NR = #count{R : input(R,_,_)}.
nc(NC) :- NC = #count{C : input(_,C,_)}.

% 2.  Build the output.  The auxiliary predicate `output_cell(R,C)` marks
%     exactly one output fact for each position (R,C).  For a given block
%     we either emit a zero cell (source colour 0) or the copied colour
%     from the tile (source colour ≠ 0).
output_cell(R,C) :-               % block whose source colour is 0
    input(BR,BC,0),
    R = BR*NR + DR,
    C = BC*NC + DC,
    output(R,C,0).

output_cell(R,C) :-               % block whose source colour is non‑zero
    input(BR,BC,Vsrc),
    input(DR,DC,Vtile),
    Vsrc != 0,
    R = BR*NR + DR,
    C = BC*NC + DC,
    output(R,C,Vtile).

% 3.  Exactly one colour for each output cell.
%     The `output` facts are already forced to be unique by the
%     definition of `output_cell`.  The cardinality statement guarantees
%     that exactly one `output` fact with a colour from 0..9 is present.
1 { output(R,C,Col) : color(Col) } 1 :- output_cell(R,C).

% Count distinct row/col indices — equals grid dimensions for 0-indexed inputs
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{R : input(R, _, _)}.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{C : input(_, C, _)}.

% Output is NR*NR rows and NC*NC cols (input tiled by itself)
output_cell(R, C) :-
    input(BR, BC, _), input(DR, DC, _),
    n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
    R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC.

1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  Transformation rule:
%   * The highest colour (4) forms the “wall”.
%   * Every cell gets a colour equal to (4 – Manhattan distance)
%     to the nearest wall cell (minimum distance → highest colour).
%   * Cells farther than distance 4 become 0.
%   * The output grid is exactly the set of cells for which the
%     formula yields a colour in 0..4; all other cells are 0.
% --------------------------------------------------------------

% All colour values that may appear (0..9 are injected automatically)
color(0). color(1). color(2). color(3). color(4). color(5).
color(6). color(7). color(8). color(9).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  1.  Identify the wall cells – the cells that originally contain
%      the maximum colour (4).  In the given puzzles these are the
%      four corner cells, but the rule works for any set of wall
%      cells.
% --------------------------------------------------------------
wall(R,C) :-
    input(R,C,4).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  2.  Manhattan distance from any cell to a wall cell.
%      ManhattanDist(R,C,D) is the distance to the *nearest* wall.
%      We first compute the distance to each wall cell, then we
%      choose the smallest distance (i.e. the largest colour).
% --------------------------------------------------------------
dist(R,C,0) :-
    wall(Wr,Cw),
    R = Wr, C = Cw.               % distance 0 for a wall cell

dist(R,C,D) :-
    wall(Wr,Cw),
    R != Wr,
    C != Cw,
    D1 = abs(R - Wr),
    D2 = abs(C - Cw),
    D3 = D1 + D2,
    D = D3.

% Helper for absolute difference.
abs(X,Y,Z) :-
    X >= Y, Z = X - Y.
abs(X,Y,Z) :-
    X <  Y, Z = Y - X.

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  3.  Derive the output colour.
%      colour = max(0, 4 - distance).
% --------------------------------------------------------------
output(R,C,V) :-
    dist(R,C,D),
    V = 4 - D,
    V >= 0,
    color(V).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  4.  Exactly one colour per cell.
% --------------------------------------------------------------
1 { output(R,C,Col) : color(Col) } 1 :- true.
</asp>

<asp>
% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  Transformation rule:
%   * The highest colour (4) forms the “wall”.
%   * Every cell gets a colour equal to (4 – Manhattan distance)
%     to the nearest wall cell (minimum distance → highest colour).
%   * Cells farther than distance 4 become 0.
%   * The output grid is exactly the set of cells for which the
%     formula yields a colour in 0..4; all other cells are 0.
% --------------------------------------------------------------

% All colour values that may appear (0..9 are injected automatically)
color(0). color(1). color(2). color(3). color(4). color(5).
color(6). color(7). color(8). color(9).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  1.  Identify the wall cells – the cells that originally contain
%      the maximum colour (4).  In the given puzzles these are the
%      four corner cells, but the rule works for any set of wall
%      cells.
% --------------------------------------------------------------
wall(R,C) :-
    input(R,C,4).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  2.  Manhattan distance from any cell to a wall cell.
%      ManhattanDist(R,C,D) is the distance to the *nearest* wall.
%      We first compute the distance to each wall cell, then we
%      choose the smallest distance (i.e. the largest colour).
% --------------------------------------------------------------
dist(R,C,0) :-
    wall(Wr,Cw),
    R = Wr, C = Cw.               % distance 0 for a wall cell

dist(R,C,D) :-
    wall(Wr,Cw),
    R != Wr,
    C != Cw,
    D1 = abs(R - Wr),
    D2 = abs(C - Cw),
    D3 = D1 + D2,
    D = D3.

% Helper for absolute difference.
abs(X,Y,Z) :-
    X >= Y, Z = X - Y.
abs(X,Y,Z) :-
    X <  Y, Z = Y - X.

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  3.  Derive the output colour.
%      colour = max(0, 4 - distance).
% --------------------------------------------------------------
output(R,C,V) :-
    dist(R,C,D),
    V = 4 - D,
    V >= 0,
    color(V).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  4.  Exactly one colour per cell.
% --------------------------------------------------------------
1 { output(R,C,Col) : color(Col) } 1 :- true.
</asp>

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- input(R, C, _).
1 { output(R, C, Col) : color(Col) } 1 :- true.

% Grid boundary coordinates
min_row(R) :- R = #min{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
max_row(R) :- R = #max{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
min_col(C) :- C = #min{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.
max_col(C) :- C = #max{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.

% 4‑connected adjacency offsets
:- delta(0,1). delta(0,-1). delta(1,0). delta(-1,0).

% Cells on the boundary that are not colour 3 are reachable from outside
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_row(Rmin), R = Rmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_row(Rmax), R = Rmax.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_col(Cmin), C = Cmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_col(Cmax), C = Cmax.

% Flood‑fill outward through cells that are not colour 3
outside(R2, C2) :-
    outside(R1, C1), delta(DR, DC),
    R2 = R1+DR, C2 = C1+DC,
    input(R2, C2, V), V != 3.

% Colour 3 cells must stay 3
:- input(R, C, 3), output(R, C, Col), Col != 3.

% Cells that are reachable from the boundary must be 0
:- outside(R, C), output(R, C, Col), Col != 0.

% Interior non‑3 cells (enclosed by colour 3 walls) become colour 4
:- input(R, C, 0), not outside(R, C), output(R, C, Col), Col != 4.
</asp>

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  Transformation rule:
%   * The highest colour (4) forms the “wall”.
%   * Every cell gets a colour equal to (4 – Manhattan distance)
%     to the nearest wall cell (minimum distance → highest colour).
%   * Cells farther than distance 4 become 0.
%   * The output grid is exactly the set of cells for which the
%     formula yields a colour in 0..4; all other cells are 0.
% --------------------------------------------------------------

% All colour values that may appear (0..9 are injected automatically)
color(0). color(1). color(2). color(3). color(4). color(5).
color(6). color(7). color(8). color(9).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  1.  Identify the wall cells – the cells that originally contain
%      the maximum colour (4).  In the given puzzles these are the
%      four corner cells, but the rule works for any set of wall
%      cells.
% --------------------------------------------------------------
wall(R,C) :-
    input(R,C,4).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  2.  Manhattan distance from any cell to a wall cell.
%      ManhattanDist(R,C,D) is the distance to the *nearest* wall.
%      We first compute the distance to each wall cell, then we
%      choose the smallest distance (i.e. the largest colour).
% --------------------------------------------------------------
dist(R,C,0) :-
    wall(Wr,Cw),
    R = Wr, C = Cw.               % distance 0 for a wall cell

dist(R,C,D) :-
    wall(Wr,Cw),
    R != Wr,
    C != Cw,
    D1 = abs(R - Wr),
    D2 = abs(C - Cw),
    D3 = D1 + D2,
    D = D3.

% Helper for absolute difference.
abs(X,Y,Z) :-
    X >= Y, Z = X - Y.
abs(X,Y,Z) :-
    X <  Y, Z = Y - X.

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  3.  Derive the output colour.
%      colour = max(0, 4 - distance).
% --------------------------------------------------------------
output(R,C,V) :-
    dist(R,C,D),
    V = 4 - D,
    V >= 0,
    color(V).

% --------------------------------------------------------------
%  4.  Exactly one colour per cell.
% --------------------------------------------------------------
1 { output(R,C,Col) : color(Col) } 1 :- true.
</asp>

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- input(R, C, _).
1 { output(R, C, Col) : color(Col) } 1 :- true.

% Grid boundary coordinates
min_row(R) :- R = #min{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
max_row(R) :- R = #max{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
min_col(C) :- C = #min{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.
max_col(C) :- C = #max{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.

% 4‑connected adjacency offsets
:- delta(0,1). delta(0,-1). delta(1,0). delta(-1,0).

% Cells on the boundary that are not colour 3 are reachable from outside
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_row(Rmin), R = Rmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_row(Rmax), R = Rmax.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_col(Cmin), C = Cmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_col(Cmax), C = Cmax.

% Flood‑fill outward through cells that are not colour 3
outside(R2, C2) :-
    outside(R1, C1), delta(DR, DC),
    R2 = R1+DR, C2 = C1+DC,
    input(R2, C2, V), V != 3.

% Colour 3 cells must stay 3
:- input(R, C, 3), output(R, C, Col), Col != 3.

% Cells that are reachable from the boundary must be 0
:- outside(R, C), output(R, C, Col), Col != 0.

% Interior non‑3 cells (enclosed by colour 3 walls) become colour 4
:- input(R, C, 0), not outside(R, C), output(R, C, Col), Col != 4.
</asp>
